diagnostic_evidence.quote: Thus, the conjugated square of the first right-singular vector is oriented as the sum of the squares of vectors $v_i$ and $v_j$.

issues.failure_explanation: Pairwise non-collinear vectors a,b,c in R^2 need not have pairwise non-collinear sums. Take a=(1,0), b=(0,1), c=(1,2); each is the complex square of a real vector, they are pairwise non-collinear, but a+b=(1,1) and a+c=(2,2) are parallel. By the displayed angle formula, parallel sums give the same first right-singular vector for the matrices built from (v1,v2) and (v1,v3), contradicting the lemma.

failure_location.quote: Since $v_1^2$, $v_2^2$ and $v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear, their sums $v_1^2 + v_2^2$, $v_1^2 + v_3^2$ and $v_2^2 + v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear too, which finalizes the proof of the lemma.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the false implication by the statement actually needed for equality triples: if a,b,c are pairwise non-collinear and satisfy p a+q b+r c=0 with p,q,r>0, then no two of a+b, a+c, b+c are positive multiples; the only possible collinear case is an opposite multiple, which still leaves the ordered first and second right-singular vectors distinct. Prove this sign argument instead.
issues.overall_effect: Lemma le is false as stated. The Case A step using it to conclude that (±1,0) can be a right-singular vector of at most one of the three equality submatrices is unsupported; through pr, the equality criteria restated in co are not established unless a stronger positive-relation version of the lemma is proved.
issues.title: Lemma le asserts a false pairwise-sum non-collinearity implication
issues.why_classification: The displayed lemma has an explicit counterexample, so a new contained argument or hypothesis is needed; however the main equality application is expected to survive under the additional positive-relation structure, so this is not a loss of the advertised result.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \hat{C} = \left( \begin{matrix} t B_{21} & B_{22} \\ \dots & \dots \\ t B_{n1} & B_{n2} \end{matrix} \right).

issues.failure_explanation: With t as displayed, \hat C^T\hat C = diag(t^2(1-b^2),1)=diag(1/(1-b^2),1), not the identity, so the inductive hypothesis is not applicable to \hat C as written. The same display also uses 1/t^2=1-b^2, whereas t=1/(1-b^2) gives 1/t^2=(1-b^2)^2. The forced normalization is t=(1-b^2)^(-1/2).

failure_location.quote: Multiplying its first column by $t = \frac{1}{1 - b^2} > 1$ we get the orthogonal matrix

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change the definition to t=(1-b^2)^(-1/2), i.e. normalize the first column of C by its norm; then \hat C is orthogonal and the later identity 1/t^2=1-b^2 is correct.
issues.overall_effect: Taken literally, the reduced matrix in Case A is not orthogonal and the induction hypothesis is misapplied; the lower-bound display is internally inconsistent. After the one-symbol normalization repair, the estimate sigma_2^2 >= 1/n and the strictness argument are unchanged.
issues.title: Case A scaling factor t does not make the reduced matrix orthogonal
issues.why_classification: The repair is a single forced normalization and preserves the method, conclusion, rate, and scope; no new lemma or reoptimization is required.

issues.failure_explanation: In the chain, the last inequality is (1-b^2)/(n-1) >= (1-1/n)/(n-1); equality requires 1-b^2 = 1-1/n, i.e. b^2=1/n or b=1/sqrt(n). As written, b=1/n gives b^2=1/n^2, for which the final inequality is already strict, so the stated equality condition is wrong.

failure_location.quote:
The equality in (\ref{ineq}) is achieved if and only if

(i) $b = \frac{1}{n}$,

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace condition (i) by b^2=1/n, equivalently b=1/sqrt(n), so that equality in the last inequality is the intended boundary case.
issues.overall_effect: Only the equality-condition list in Case A is misstated. The strictness conclusion for Case A survives because b=1/n is already inside the strict regime, but the boundary case b^2=1/n must be corrected for the induction-equality argument to be valid.
issues.title: Case A equality boundary condition should be b^2=1/n, not b=1/n
issues.why_classification: This is a one-symbol boundary correction; the strictness conclusion and the equality criteria survive without any change of method or loss of regime.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: three non-empty groups of $p, \, q, \, r > 0$

issues.failure_explanation: The equality criteria allow p=1, and similarly q=1 or r=1. For a singleton block there are not two vectors to select, so the displayed pairwise argument does not by itself yield the magnitude for that block. The magnitude is still forced by the diagonal of the uniform block: for i in a block of size p, M_ii=2/(pn) while M_ii=4|w_i|/n-2/n^2, hence |w_i|=1/(2n)+1/(2p).

failure_location.quote: Let us select from $w_1, \ldots, w_n$ two vectors corresponding to the first block of (\ref{blck}) and denote them by $u$ and $v$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Handle blocks of size 1 separately, or read the magnitude directly from the diagonal of the uniform block in the displayed block matrix; for blocks of size at least two keep the pairwise argument.
issues.overall_effect: As written, the final equality derivation does not cover singleton equality blocks; the conclusion remains available from the block-diagonal entries, so the equality criteria survive once this degenerate case is handled.
issues.title: Equality derivation assumes each block has two vectors, missing singleton blocks
issues.why_classification: This is a local degenerate-case gap with an immediate repair from the already displayed uniform block structure; no substantive claim or rate is lost.
